questions.q: Which statement best defines cardiomyopathy?
ch: A myocardial disorder causing structural, mechanical, or electrical dysfunction not explained solely by coronary, valve, hypertensive, or congenital disease
A congenital malformation of a heart valve
A transient rhythm disturbance without myocardial disease
Any myocardial dysfunction caused by obstructive coronary artery disease

questions.q: Which finding most strongly supports a dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype?
ch: Unexplained asymmetric septal hypertrophy with dynamic outflow obstruction
Small ventricular cavities with marked biatrial enlargement and preserved ejection fraction
Isolated valve calcification with normal ventricular function
Left-ventricular or biventricular dilation with reduced systolic function

questions.q: Which combination is most characteristic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
ch: Thin ventricular walls, severe chamber dilation, and isolated right-sided valve disease
Normal myocardium with an isolated pericardial effusion
Small atria with normal diastolic filling and low arrhythmic risk
Unexplained ventricular hypertrophy, impaired relaxation, and possible dynamic left-ventricular outflow obstruction

questions.q: Which pattern best describes restrictive cardiomyopathy early in its course?
ch: Isolated enlargement of the ascending aorta
Transient ventricular dysfunction after emotional stress only
Markedly dilated ventricles with severe systolic dysfunction in every case
Normal or small ventricles, impaired filling, biatrial enlargement, and potentially preserved ejection fraction

questions.q: Which feature is most typical of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy?
ch: Reversible pericardial inflammation without myocardial injury
Ventricular scar or fibrofatty disease with ventricular arrhythmias that may precede heart failure
Purely atrial disease without ventricular involvement

questions.q: Which cause of ventricular dysfunction is often at least partially reversible when the underlying problem is corrected?
ch: A fixed congenital absence of the pericardium
Long-standing calcific aortic stenosis without intervention
An inherited sarcomeric variant in every affected patient
Persistent rapid tachyarrhythmia causing tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy

questions.q: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which maneuver commonly makes the systolic murmur louder?
ch: Standing suddenly or performing the Valsalva maneuver
Increasing venous return with fluid loading

questions.q: What is the usual first-line imaging test when cardiomyopathy is suspected?
ch: Coronary angiography as the only initial test

questions.q: What is a major reason to obtain cardiac magnetic resonance imaging in cardiomyopathy?
ch: To replace the clinical history and pedigree
To characterize myocardial tissue, scar, edema, infiltration, and anatomy
To diagnose every inherited variant without genetic testing
To measure blood pressure more accurately

questions.q: An older adult has increased ventricular wall thickness and suspected cardiac amyloidosis. Which sequence is most appropriate before using bone-avid tracer scintigraphy to support ATTR amyloidosis?
ch: Serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation; proceed to scintigraphy if no monoclonal protein is detected
Exercise ECG followed by chest radiography
Start disease-specific treatment without defining the amyloid type
Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy first, with no laboratory testing

questions.q: Which group represents the four foundational medication classes for chronic HFrEF when tolerated?
ch: ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor
Loop diuretic, aspirin, statin, and calcium supplement
Nitrate, digoxin, anticoagulant, and antiarrhythmic for every patient

questions.q: A patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy develops atrial fibrillation. Which statement is most accurate?
ch: Anticoagulation is generally indicated regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score, unless contraindicated
Anticoagulation is never used because HCM is not thromboembolic
Anticoagulation is considered only after a second stroke
A normal ejection fraction eliminates thromboembolic risk

questions.q: Which findings may occur in cardiomyopathy? Select all that apply.
ch: Elevated jugular venous pressure or peripheral edema
A localized skin rash as the defining cardiac manifestation

questions.q: Which findings should trigger urgent evaluation in a patient with known or suspected cardiomyopathy? Select all that apply.
ch: Sustained ventricular tachycardia or cardiac arrest
Acute pulmonary edema, hypotension, or shock
Stable mild fatigue unchanged for months

questions.q: Which cardiomyopathy forms or causes may improve substantially when the trigger is removed or treated? Select all that apply.
ch: Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy after effective rate or rhythm control
Toxic or therapy-related cardiomyopathy after exposure recognition and appropriate management
Peripartum cardiomyopathy in some patients with pregnancy-aware heart-failure care
Uncomplicated hypertension without a myocardial phenotype

questions.q: Which actions belong in the evaluation of possible inherited cardiomyopathy? Select all that apply.
ch: Use genetic counseling and testing when inherited disease is suspected
Screen first-degree relatives according to phenotype, age, and family context
Wait for relatives to become symptomatic before discussing screening

questions.q: Case: A 22-year-old with HCM has no symptoms and asks about exercise. Which counseling is most consistent with current guidance?
ch: Healthy recreational exercise is encouraged; rigorous competitive training should be individualized through shared decision-making and periodic expert reevaluation
Competitive exercise is automatically safe without risk assessment
Exercise advice is unrelated to HCM phenotype or arrhythmic risk

questions.q: Case: A 76-year-old has exertional dyspnea, increased ventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and ECG voltage that appears low relative to wall thickness. Which process should be strongly considered?
ch: A normal age-related finding requiring no further evaluation
Cardiac amyloidosis causing an infiltrative/restrictive phenotype

questions.q: Case: A patient develops new dilated cardiomyopathy after anthracycline exposure. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
ch: The diagnosis must be HCM because the patient received cancer therapy
Family screening replaces assessment of the treatment exposure
Therapy-related myocardial injury is a plausible cause and the exposure history should guide evaluation and management
The exposure is irrelevant once ventricular dilation is visible

questions.q: Case: A patient with symptomatic obstructive HCM remains limited despite an appropriate first-line nonvasodilating beta-blocker. What is the best next general strategy?
ch: Treat the patient as uncomplicated HFrEF without reassessing obstruction
Stop all therapy and observe indefinitely
Refer for specialty-directed escalation, which may include a cardiac myosin inhibitor or other therapy and consideration of expert septal reduction when refractory
Use large, unmonitored preload reductions to increase the obstruction

questions.q: Which statement best characterizes peripheral arterial disease (PAD)?
ch: Lymphatic obstruction producing non-pitting limb swelling with thickened overlying skin
Atherosclerotic narrowing of the limb arteries causing exertional claudication and marking systemic cardiovascular risk
Venous valve incompetence producing dependent edema and stasis pigmentation of the calf
Inflammatory small-vessel vasculitis confined to the digital arteries of the hands
Acute thrombosis of the deep calf veins presenting with unilateral swelling and tenderness

questions.q: Which resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) value is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease?
Which set of findings makes up the '6 Ps' of acute limb ischemia?
ch: Pain, pruritus, purpura, pallor, pitting edema, pulsatility
Pallor, palpitations, pyrexia, paralysis, petechiae, pain
Paresthesia, pyuria, pallor, pain, photophobia, pulselessness
Pain, pallor, polyuria, pulselessness, pruritus, paresis
Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia

questions.q: A man with long-standing diabetes and chronic kidney disease has classic calf claudication, but his resting ABI is 1.48. What is the best next step?
ch: Proceed directly to surgical bypass of the femoropopliteal segment
Obtain CT angiography of the lower extremities as a screening test
Toe-brachial index, because medial calcification makes the ankle vessels non-compressible
Repeat the resting ABI in one week and accept the result if it is unchanged
Reassure him that an ABI above 1.40 excludes peripheral arterial disease

questions.q: Which agent is the first-line symptomatic drug to increase pain-free walking distance in claudication, yet is contraindicated in heart failure?
A 64-year-old smoker reports cramping buttock and hip pain with walking, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses. Where is the lesion?
Which treatment for intermittent claudication is a Class I, guideline first-line recommendation that improves walking distance as much as many drugs?
ch: Chronic warfarin anticoagulation targeting an INR of 2 to 3
Graduated compression stockings worn during all waking hours
Elevating both legs above heart level for an hour each day
Supervised exercise therapy — a structured walking program
Strict bed rest until the leg pain resolves completely

questions.q: A patient with known PAD now wakes at night with foot pain that improves when he hangs the foot off the side of the bed. What does this indicate?
ch: Critical limb-threatening ischemia with rest pain, needing urgent vascular referral
Simple nocturnal leg cramps requiring only stretching and better hydration
Improving collateral circulation and a favorable response to a walking program
Deep vein thrombosis of the calf, best confirmed with duplex ultrasound
Neurogenic pseudoclaudication arising from lumbar spinal stenosis

questions.q: A 70-year-old has leg pain with walking that is relieved only by sitting or bending forward; his pedal pulses and ABI are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
ch: Atheroembolism causing blue toe syndrome, with mottled toes and intact proximal pulses
Neurogenic pseudoclaudication from spinal stenosis, relieved by flexion rather than by rest alone
Aortoiliac Leriche disease, which typically abolishes the femoral pulses and lowers the ABI
Critical limb-threatening ischemia, which causes rest pain and ulceration rather than exertional pain
Acute limb ischemia, which presents abruptly with the 6 Ps including pulselessness and pallor

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the prognosis of symptomatic PAD and the lipid goal that follows from it?
ch: PAD risk is confined to the limb, so the lipid target is the same as for the general population
Amputation is the leading cause of death in PAD, so a statin adds little beyond exercise therapy
Statins should be avoided in PAD because myalgias limit walking distance in claudication
Lipid lowering is indicated only after revascularization has failed to relieve the symptoms
PAD is a coronary heart disease risk equivalent — most patients die of MI or stroke — so a high-intensity statin targeting LDL below 70 mg/dL is recommended

questions.q: Which veins are most commonly involved in clinically significant lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis?
ch: Posterior tibial and peroneal veins only

questions.q: Virchow's triad consists of which three major contributors to venous thrombosis?
ch: Hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury

questions.q: Which symptom is most commonly associated with acute lower-extremity DVT?
Which physical examination finding is considered most suggestive of DVT?
ch: Localized calf tenderness with unilateral swelling

questions.q: What is the first-line imaging study for suspected lower-extremity DVT?
Which histologic component predominates in a venous thrombus?
ch: Fibrin and trapped red blood cells

questions.q: What is the most serious complication of untreated DVT?
Which medication class is recommended as first-line treatment for most patients with acute DVT?
Which patient has the greatest risk for developing DVT?
ch: Recent major orthopedic surgery with prolonged immobilization

questions.q: Which statement best summarizes modern DVT management?
ch: Early diagnosis and anticoagulation prevent pulmonary embolism and long-term complications.

questions.q: Which layer of the aortic wall first tears in an acute aortic dissection?
Which classification system is most commonly used for aortic dissections?
Which symptom is most characteristic of acute aortic dissection?
ch: Sudden severe tearing chest or back pain

questions.q: Which imaging study is preferred for a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected aortic dissection?
What is the major goal of initial medical management for acute aortic dissection?
ch: Lower blood pressure and reduce shear stress

questions.q: Which inherited disorder is strongly associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm?
Which physical examination finding may occur in proximal (Type A) aortic dissection?
Which complication is most feared with an enlarging abdominal aortic aneurysm?
Which treatment is definitive for most Stanford Type A dissections?
What is the most important long-term management strategy after successful treatment of aortic aneurysm or dissection?
ch: Lifelong blood pressure control and surveillance imaging

questions.q: A patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite carotid pulse within 10 seconds. What is the next step?
Recommended adult chest compression rate is:
Which rhythm is shockable?
Primary purpose of high-quality CPR is:
Which is NOT one of the Hs and Ts?
During adult cardiac arrest, epinephrine dose is:
With an advanced airway in place:
ch: Continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 sec

questions.q: An abrupt sustained rise in ETCOI during CPR most likely indicates:
After ROSC, an appropriate MAP target is:
Which statement best summarizes ACLS priorities?
ch: CPR and early defibrillation are the highest priorities

questions.q: Which mechanism best explains how elevated LDL-C causes atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
ch: Retained ApoB-containing particles enter the arterial intima, oxidize, and trigger foam-cell and plaque formation
Cholesterol crystals precipitate directly within the cardiac valves and produce stenosis
Excess circulating lipid raises blood viscosity enough to mechanically obstruct the arteries
Triglycerides are deposited within the myocardium and progressively impair contractile function
HDL particles carry cholesterol into the vessel wall, where it accumulates as fatty streaks

questions.q: A 32-year-old with an untreated LDL-C of 245 mg/dL has thickened Achilles tendons and firm nodules over the knuckles. What do these findings indicate?
ch: Corneal arcus, an entirely expected age-related change
Gouty tophi, reflecting chronically elevated serum uric acid
Tendon xanthomas, the classic sign of familial hypercholesterolemia
Eruptive xanthomas, which accompany severe hypertriglyceridemia
Xanthelasma, a periorbital deposit without lipid significance

questions.q: By what mechanism do statins lower LDL-C?
ch: They activate PPAR-alpha and thereby accelerate triglyceride clearance
They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors
They block intestinal cholesterol absorption at the brush border
They inhibit ATP-citrate lyase upstream of hepatic cholesterol synthesis
They are monoclonal antibodies that neutralize circulating PCSK9

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four AHA/ACC statin benefit groups?
ch: Isolated triglycerides of 200 mg/dL on a fasting panel
Any adult over the age of 40 regardless of risk factors
A total cholesterol above 180 mg/dL in a nonsmoking adult
Untreated LDL-C of 190 mg/dL or higher at any age
An HDL-C below 40 mg/dL in an otherwise healthy adult

questions.q: A patient's triglycerides return at 1,200 mg/dL and he has epigastric pain. Which risk does this represent, and which drug class targets it?
ch: Cholestatic liver injury — treated with observation and imaging
Acute pancreatitis — treated with a fibrate such as fenofibrate
Accelerated atherosclerosis — treated with a PCSK9 inhibitor
Rhabdomyolysis — treated by stopping all lipid-lowering therapy
Hypothyroid myopathy — treated with levothyroxine replacement

questions.q: Which drug combination carries the greatest risk of dangerous myopathy in a patient who needs both LDL and triglyceride lowering?
A very high-risk ASCVD patient is not at LDL goal on a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin. What is the next step in the titration sequence?
ch: Stop the statin and start a fibrate as monotherapy instead
Add niacin and recheck the lipid panel in one year's time
Escalate the statin beyond the maximally tolerated dose
Defer any further therapy until a repeat CAC score is obtained
Add ezetimibe, then a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid if still not at goal

questions.q: A patient taking atorvastatin reports severe muscle pain, weakness, and dark tea-colored urine. What is the priority concern?
ch: Tendon rupture, the characteristic risk of bempedoic acid therapy
Statin hepatotoxicity, which baseline LFTs would have predicted
Dehydration producing concentrated but otherwise normal urine
Rhabdomyolysis — a red flag requiring immediate evaluation
Ordinary statin-associated muscle symptoms; continue unchanged

questions.q: How is the coronary artery calcium (CAC) score best used in lipid management?
ch: To reclassify intermediate-risk patients when the statin treatment decision is uncertain
To replace the lipid panel as the primary screening test for dyslipidemia
To confirm familial hypercholesterolemia in a patient with tendon xanthomas
To monitor the response to therapy every three months after starting a statin
To decide whether triglyceride lowering is needed to prevent acute pancreatitis

questions.q: A previously well patient is found to have new, marked hyperlipidemia. Which workup best screens for secondary causes?
ch: Abdominal ultrasound and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
A genetic panel for PCSK9 gain-of-function mutations in every patient
TSH, fasting glucose or HbA1c, renal and liver panel, and urine protein
Coronary angiography together with an exercise treadmill test
Serum CK and an electromyogram of the proximal muscle groups

questions.q: What is the fundamental abnormality in ARDS?
ch: Left ventricular failure raising pulmonary capillary pressure
Increased alveolar-capillary permeability flooding alveoli with protein-rich fluid
Obstruction of the pulmonary arteries by thrombus

questions.q: Which parameter does the Berlin definition use to stage ARDS severity?
ch: The PaO2/FiO2 ratio on PEEP of at least 5
Peak airway pressure measured at end-inspiration
Serum lactate corrected for cardiac output
Tidal volume per kilogram of predicted body weight

questions.q: Which two causes are the most common triggers of ARDS?
What is the cornerstone ventilatory strategy in ARDS?
ch: High tidal volumes to recruit collapsed lung
Low tidal volume of 6 mL/kg predicted body weight with a limited plateau pressure
Tidal volume set by the patient's actual body weight

questions.q: Why does raising the FiO2 alone often fail to correct hypoxemia in ARDS?
ch: Because reduced cardiac output limits oxygen delivery to the tissues
Because methemoglobin cannot bind oxygen at normal partial pressures
Because increased dead space prevents carbon dioxide clearance
Because intrapulmonary shunt means blood bypasses ventilated alveoli
Because carbon monoxide is occupying the haemoglobin binding sites

questions.q: What does the term 'baby lung' describe in ARDS?
ch: The characteristic appearance of the lung on bedside ultrasound
ARDS occurring in paediatric rather than adult patients
That only a small fraction of lung remains aerated, so normal tidal volumes overdistend it
The reduced lung volume remaining after a lobectomy
Congenital surfactant deficiency in the newborn lung

questions.q: Which intervention has been shown to improve survival in severe ARDS?
A ventilated ARDS patient suddenly desaturates with rising airway pressures and hypotension. What should be suspected first?
A patient develops ARDS within 6 hours of receiving a blood product. What should be considered?
A patient with severe ARDS remains profoundly hypoxemic despite optimised PEEP, proning and neuromuscular blockade. What is the appropriate next escalation?
ch: Accept the hypoxemia and continue current settings
Increase tidal volume to improve minute ventilation

questions.q: Why does the lung collapse when air enters the pleural space?
ch: The bronchi constrict and trap air distally
The diaphragm becomes paralysed on the affected side
Surfactant is inactivated and the alveoli collapse
The alveoli fill with protein-rich fluid
The negative intrapleural pressure is lost and the lung recoils inward

questions.q: Which patient fits the classic description of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
ch: A patient who has just had a central line placed
An elderly patient with severe COPD
A tall, thin young male smoker

questions.q: In which direction does the trachea deviate in a tension pneumothorax?
A hypotensive patient has absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side with distended neck veins. What is the correct immediate action?
ch: Give a fluid bolus and reassess in 15 minutes
Obtain an urgent chest X-ray to confirm

questions.q: Why is high-flow supplemental oxygen given in pneumothorax?
ch: It is required before any chest tube insertion
It accelerates reabsorption of pleural air by nitrogen washout
It prevents infection of the pleural space

questions.q: Which bedside ultrasound finding suggests pneumothorax?
ch: Absence of lung sliding with a barcode sign on M-mode

questions.q: A supine trauma patient may show which subtle radiographic sign of pneumothorax?
What does recent evidence suggest about management of many primary spontaneous pneumothoraces?
ch: All require immediate large-bore chest tube drainage
Conservative watchful waiting is non-inferior in many cases
All require surgical pleurodesis at first presentation

questions.q: Which patient is least suitable for observation alone and most likely to need a chest tube?
ch: A patient with underlying COPD and a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
A patient whose pneumothorax has already resolved on repeat film
A patient with a resolved iatrogenic pneumothorax after line removal
An asymptomatic patient with normal saturations and a tiny apical rim
A young patient with a small asymptomatic primary pneumothorax

questions.q: A patient who is a commercial diver has had a second spontaneous pneumothorax. What definitive management should be considered?
ch: Pleurodesis or VATS with bleb resection
